candidates.raw_excerpt: The Army’s first class of permanent enlisted space warfighters is now reporting for duty. On Oct. 1, 600+ soldiers swapped their old jobs for the new 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialist military occupational specialty (MOS). “We had nearly 3,000 soldiers apply, and selected over 600 of the most capable, professional soldiers in the Army,” said Command Sgt. Maj. Rickey Jackson of US Army Space and Missile Defense Command (USASMDC) in a statement. The 40D specialists are the enlisted counterpart to the Functional Area 40A Space Operations Officers, who have been part of the Army since 1999. Home branch: The Army previously filled space-ops assignments by temporarily shifting soldiers from other specialities, losing that expertise when they returned to their home branch. The 40D MOS creates a permanent supply of enlisted space specialists. The two cohorts now share a home in the Army’s Space Operations Branch , established in June to consolidate the career paths of the service’s space professionals. “For 27 years, Army space officers have been working to normalize Army space operations, and that’s what this branch designation now does for the Army,” Brig. Gen. Donald K. Brooks, USASMDC’s deputy commanding general, said in a statement. Marching orders: The Army says the branch brings the 2024 Army Space Vision to fruition. The document directed the service to focus on integrating joint, coalition, and commercial space capabilities and interdicting adversary space capabilities to protect friendly forces.  The 40D MOS puts that into practice: Training takes place at the Space and Missile Defense Center of Excellence in Colorado Springs, CO—preparing soldiers for space integration and interdiction missions, including counter-satcom, stratospheric warfare, navigation warfare, and counter-sensing. The well is designed to explore the oil and gas potential of large structural traps in the deep northwestern Tarim Basin, particularly those dating back to the Sinian Period, and to identify new areas for expanding oil and gas reserves.

The 12,000-meter rig features an 82-meter-high steel derrick capable of handling a maximum load of 665 tonnes and is designed to drill to depths of up to 12,000 meters. Its development means China no longer needs to rely on imported rigs for drilling wells deeper than 10,000 meters.

This marks the rig's second successful application. Equipped with a 6,000-horsepower drilling drawworks, the most powerful of its kind in China, and a 900-tonne lifting system, the rig can lift a load equivalent to two high-speed train sets.
